title: How a hash map resolves a collision (separate chaining)
summary: Three keys go into a hash map with four buckets. Two of them land in the same bucket. Watch how the map stores both, finds the right one again, and what a lookup for a missing key does.

zones.label: The table: an array of 4 buckets

steps.label: put("cat", 7)
steps.title: The program stores "cat" with the value 7
steps.desc: A hash map stores key and value pairs in an array of buckets. To decide which bucket, it turns the key into a number.

steps.label: hash("cat") = 312, bucket 0
steps.title: The map hashes the key to pick a bucket
steps.desc: This example uses a toy hash: add up the character codes of the key. The bucket index is the remainder after dividing by the number of buckets. 312 mod 4 = 0.
notes: The same key always gives the same bucket. That is what makes lookups fast: the map goes straight to one bucket instead of searching all of them.

steps.label: insert cat = 7
steps.title: Bucket 0 is empty, so the entry goes in
steps.desc: The map creates an entry holding both the key and the value and puts it in bucket 0. The key is stored too, not just the value. A later step shows why.

steps.label: put("dog", 3)
steps.title: The program stores "dog" with the value 3
steps.desc: A second key. The map repeats the same two moves: hash, then go to that bucket.

steps.label: hash("dog") = 314, bucket 2
steps.title: A different key usually gives a different bucket

steps.label: insert dog = 3
steps.title: Bucket 2 is empty, so the entry goes in
steps.desc: No other entry is in the way. So far every key has had a bucket to itself.

steps.label: put("act", 9)
steps.title: The program stores "act" with the value 9
steps.desc: A third key. It is made of the same letters as "cat", in a different order.

steps.label: hash("act") = 312, bucket 0
steps.title: Two different keys hash to the same bucket
steps.desc: Adding the same three character codes in another order gives the same sum, 312, and the same bucket, 0. This is a collision. With more possible keys than buckets, collisions cannot be avoided, only made rare.
notes: A real hash function mixes the position of each character into the result, so "cat" and "act" would differ. Collisions still happen, because many hash values share each bucket.

steps.label: act = 9 goes to bucket 0
steps.title: The new entry arrives at a bucket that is taken
steps.desc: Bucket 0 already holds the entry for "cat". The map must not overwrite it: "cat" and "act" are different keys that happen to share a bucket.

steps.label: "cat" equals "act"? no
steps.title: Compare keys, then chain the new entry
steps.desc: The map compares the new key with each key already in the bucket. "cat" is not equal to "act" and there are no more entries, so this is a new key. With separate chaining, the bucket holds a linked list and the new entry is added to it.
notes: If the keys had been equal, the map would have replaced the old value instead of adding an entry.
This is why the key is stored with the value: the bucket index alone cannot tell two colliding keys apart.

steps.label: get("act")
steps.title: The program asks for "act"
steps.desc: A lookup starts exactly like an insert. The map hashes the key again: 312 mod 4 = 0.

steps.label: look for "act"
steps.title: The map goes to bucket 0
steps.desc: The hash tells the map which bucket to search. It does not say which entry in that bucket is the right one.

steps.label: "cat"? no. "act"? yes
steps.title: Walk the chain until a key matches
steps.desc: The map compares the wanted key with each entry in turn. The first entry is "cat": not equal, move on. The second is "act": equal, so this is the entry.
notes: A lookup costs one hash plus one comparison per entry in the chain. Short chains keep that close to constant time.

steps.label: found: 9
steps.title: The value 9 is returned
steps.desc: The collision cost one extra comparison, and the right value still came back.

steps.label: get("tac")
steps.title: The program asks for a key that was never stored
steps.desc: "tac" is another arrangement of the same letters. Its hash is 312 again, so the map goes to bucket 0 again.

steps.label: look for "tac"
steps.title: The map goes to bucket 0
steps.desc: The bucket is not empty, but that does not mean the key is present.

steps.label: "cat"? no. "act"? no. end
steps.title: No key in the chain matches
steps.desc: The map compares "tac" with every entry in the chain and reaches the end without a match.
steps.fail: The key "tac" was never inserted. Landing in the same bucket as other keys is not a match: only an equal key is.

steps.label: not found
steps.title: The lookup reports that the key is absent
steps.desc: What "not found" looks like depends on the language: Java's HashMap.get returns null, Python raises KeyError, Go returns the zero value and false.

simplifications: The hash function is a toy (sum of character codes) chosen so the arithmetic fits on screen. It is a poor hash: any two anagrams collide.

The table has 4 buckets and never grows. A real hash map resizes and redistributes its entries as it fills up. Java's HashMap does so once the number of entries exceeds 0.75 times the number of buckets.
Each chain is a plain linked list. Java's HashMap turns a long chain into a balanced tree to keep worst-case lookups fast.
Separate chaining is one of two common strategies. The other, open addressing, keeps every entry in the array itself and probes for another slot on a collision; Python's dict works that way.
Removing entries, replacing the value of an existing key and iteration order are not shown.
